items.title: Carter Benny — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: As you know, Glenn Miller—I’m jumping ahead a few years.

ctx.x: I’d like to move to just some general observations about your bands, and we’re going to discuss how this great 1933 orchestra began to, unfortunately, disband because of lack of work and, well, there’s a lot of economic factors and other things involved. But a lot of people through the years, writers especially, have found it uneasy discussing your career in terms of commercial success versus artistic integrity and versus musical integrity and all of that. As you said just now, you don’t really have a long-range…

No, I don’t think it was that. As I say, I just . . . I didn’t think of it along those lines, but I will admit that there are times when I had someone other than myself or other than a member of the orchestra doing arrangement here and there, thinking maybe it could be . . . lead to some commercialism or some commercial success. As you know, Glenn Miller—I’m jumping ahead a few years.

items.title: 66095_Benny Carter oral history interview
items.q: I know I did some things for Glenn Miller

ctx.x: This band -- did you have some particular motive and style of music that you wanted to get played with this band that forms in '32 and '33 and which Teddy Wilson joins?

No. I don't think I did, and I think that had another thing, maybe - had something else to do with the band not becoming a great commercial success. I don't think any band I ever had had a really identifiable Benny Carter sound. You know, like ... I think the Goodman band developed that and of course, the Glenn Miller Band,
which was not really a swing or a jazz band. They had that by virtue of the sound of the clarinet lead thing and certain other things. But I don't know; maybe ...
